title: Sam Altman Offered Washington 5% of OpenAI. The Government Wants More.
excerpt: The White House restricted GPT-5.6, lifted Anthropic's export ban, and is drafting voluntary AI standards — all in one week. Indian AI builders may feel the squeeze first.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI offered the U.S. government a 5% stake worth $42 billion.
  • The White House is tightening AI model release regulations.
  • Indian AI professionals face uncertainty due to new U.S. policies.
  • OpenAI's IPO plans hinge on managing regulatory relationships.
  • Senator Sanders advocates for a 50% government stake in AI firms.
AI Regulation Takes Center Stage
›$42 billion OpenAI proposed a 5% stake to the U.S. government.
›Limited public access White House restricted GPT-5.6 release to vetted partners.
›Fable 5 and Mythos 5 Anthropic's models faced export controls for 3 weeks.
›Announcement expected soon New voluntary standards for AI model releases are in talks.
Sam Altman has a proposition for Washington: take a 5 per cent slice of the most valuable artificial intelligence company on Earth, and perhaps the government will ease up on deciding who gets to use its products. OpenAI has proposed giving the Trump administration a stake worth roughly $42 billion at its current valuation, the Financial Times reported last week. The offer came with a twist — Altman suggested other leading AI firms hand over similar equity, a move that would effectively create a government portfolio of Silicon Valley's most powerful technologies. ![White House — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg/3840px-White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg) ## The Crackdown No One Predicted The gesture did not arrive in a vacuum. Days earlier, the White House formally asked OpenAI to restrict the release of its newest model, GPT-5.6, to a small group of government-vetted partners rather than opening it to the public. An internal memo from Altman acknowledged the company was complying with the request, even as he called the approval process unsustainable. > **"government a 5% stake worth $42 billion.
  • The White House is tightening AI model release regulations.
  • Indian AI professionals face uncertainty due to new U.S."** The intervention followed the Commerce Department's export controls on Anthropic's most advanced models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, which were pulled from circulation for nearly three weeks over fears that their cybersecurity capabilities could be weaponised by foreign adversaries. Those restrictions were lifted on 30 June, but the message was clear: the era of build-first, regulate-later in AI is over. Washington is now in advanced talks with AI companies to establish voluntary standards for model releases, Reuters reported, with an announcement potentially arriving this week. The framework would set benchmarks for advanced models and clarify who can access them, both domestically and abroad. ![Financial Times — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/8a/Financial_Times_22_February_2021_cover.jpg) ## What This Means for Indian Tech For the estimated 300,000-plus Indian professionals working in AI and adjacent roles across the United States, the regulatory pivot creates a new variable in an already uncertain landscape. Stricter model-release protocols could slow hiring at labs that are already selective, while government-directed access restrictions raise questions about which clients — and which countries — get frontier AI capabilities. Sriram Krishnan, the Indian-American entrepreneur now serving as the White House's senior AI policy advisor, sits at the centre of these negotiations. His presence ensures India's interests are at least visible in the room, but visibility is not the same as guarantee. India's own $67.5 billion AI investment push, anchored by the IndiaAI Mission's 18,000-plus GPUs, could be constrained if Washington decides its most advanced models are too sensitive for broad international deployment.
    Impact on Indian AI Sector
    ›Estimated workforce 300,000+ Indian professionals work in AI in the U.S.
    ›IndiaAI Mission India's AI investment is $67.5 billion.
    ›GPU count 18,000+ GPUs are part of India's AI infrastructure.
    ›Risk of operational delays Delays in model access could hinder Indian startups.
    ![Silicon Valley — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg) Indian AI startups like Sarvam AI and Krutrim, which depend on fine-tuning frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic, face a practical risk: if new release protocols add weeks or months before models reach international developers, India's AI builders would operate on a delay that their Chinese counterparts — who are building independent models on domestic chips — would not face. ## The IPO Calculation The stake proposal is also deeply tied to OpenAI's path toward an initial public offering. The company burned through $3.7 billion in cash in Q1 alone while tripling revenue to $5.7 billion. Managing regulatory goodwill is critical before going public — a government that owns equity is a government less likely to regulate aggressively.

    Senator Sanders' proposed stake
    Senator Bernie Sanders has pushed for a 50 per cent government stake in major AI companies, arguing the technology was trained on human knowledge used without permission. The 5 per cent offer looks like Altman drawing a line before someone else draws it higher. For NRI investors eyeing the AI sector, the calculus has shifted. These are no longer pure growth stories — they are companies navigating a regulatory environment that is evolving faster than their models. The question is no longer just how powerful the next model will be, but who gets to use it.
